strategy:
1. Approach and rationale

Optimize by deterministic, feasibility-preserving coordinate descent whose individual updates are exact one-dimensional minimizations of the original finite-lag objective. A move transfers mass between two coordinates, so its entire feasible range is an interval. Along that interval each lag sum is a quadratic; only three lag sums can be quadratic, while every other lag sum is affine. The maximum of the affine lags is a piecewise-linear upper envelope. Intersections of that envelope and the three quadratics partition the interval into pieces on which the objective is one polynomial, so a finite set of endpoints, crossings, and convex-quadratic vertices contains a global minimizer along that coordinate direction. Accept a move only after scoring its vector with the exact evaluator.

This is materially different from projected gradient with a smoothed maximum and annealed transfers, sequential LP trust regions, differential evolution, and an SLSQP epigraph solve: it does not optimize a smoothed objective, solve an LP/NLP, or use population mutation or uphill moves. Its primary operation is an exact finite candidate search over a mass-preserving coordinate line. Analytic lag derivatives are used only to form that line’s quadratic coefficients.

The finite-support lag formula, the quadratic coefficients, and the one-dimensional candidate-set argument are mathematical facts. A sparse set of coordinate pairs, multiple starts, and fixed search budgets are heuristics to control the work and explore different local basins. The full problem remains nonconvex, and coordinate descent is not a global method; no improvement over the parent, the record, or 0.3808 is guaranteed. Any improvement applies to the sampled evaluator, not by itself to a separate continuous-domain theorem.

2. Mathematical specification

For runtime length n, let h ∈ Rⁿ, dx = 2/n, and S = n/2. The feasible set is K = {h: 0 ≤ h[i] ≤ 1 for all i, and Σᵢ h[i] = S}. Keep a usable parent’s resolution unchanged.

For each integer lag d ∈ {-(n-1), …, n-1}, define lo = max(0,-d), hi = min(n,n-d), and the raw finite-support lag sum B_d(h) = Σᵢ₌ₗₒ^{hi-1} h[i](1-h[i+d]). The exact objective is C(h) = dx · max_d B_d(h). These are all 2n-1 entries of np.correlate(h, 1-h, mode='full'), possibly in reversed order. The slices exclude wraparound and use only the actual partial overlap at nonzero lags. Include both lag directions; do not use an autocorrelation identity that drops boundary terms. Since dx is positive, minimizing max_d B_d also minimizes C.

For coordinate r, the raw lag gradient is

g[d,r] = 1_{lo ≤ r < hi}(1-h[r+d]) - 1_{lo+d ≤ r < hi+d}h[r-d],

with each term included only when its indicator is true. For d=0 this is 1-2h[r].

For distinct coordinates p and q, define v = e_p-e_q and h(t)=h+t v. The complete feasible interval is

t_lo = max(-h[p], h[q]-1),   t_hi = min(1-h[p], h[q]).

It contains zero for a feasible h. Each raw lag is exactly B_d(h(t)) = c_d+b_d t+a_d t², where c_d=B_d(h), b_d=g[d,p]-g[d,q], and a_d=-Σᵢ₌ₗₒ^{hi-1}v[i]v[i+d]. With gap = q-p when p<q, the only nonzero quadratic coefficients are a_0=-2 and a_gap=a_-gap=+1; all other a_d are zero. This follows because v has nonzero entries only at p and q, so its shifted inner product is nonzero only at shift zero or the two shifts connecting the coordinates.

Let Q_d(t)=a_d t²+b_d t+c_d for the three special lags and let L(t) be the maximum of all remaining affine functions b_d t+c_d. If there are no remaining lags, define L(t)=-∞. Then the line objective is F(t)=max(L(t), Q_0(t), Q_gap(t), Q_-gap(t)). Build the upper envelope of the affine lines. Partition [t_lo,t_hi] at its breakpoints, its active-line intersections with each Q, and all pairwise intersections among the three Q curves. Within each resulting interval the active branch of F cannot change. A linear or concave-quadratic branch has its minimum at an interval endpoint; a convex-quadratic branch can also have an interior minimum only at its vertex. Therefore endpoints, all those intersections, and the vertices of the convex Q curves contain a global minimizer of F on the feasible interval. Evaluate this finite candidate set and use the exact evaluator to decide whether its resulting vector is accepted.

The joint Euclidean projection of z onto K has the form P(z)[i]=clip(z[i]-λ,0,1), with λ chosen so that ΣᵢP(z)[i]=S. This follows from the KKT conditions for squared-distance projection with one sum equality and coordinate bounds. Use this projection for arbitrary starts and numerical repairs; clipping followed by rescaling is not a valid joint feasibility method.

3. Implementation procedure

3.1. Program structure. Write one complete program defining run(seed=42, **kwargs) at top level. Define every helper at top level; do not use closures or lambdas. NumPy and math suffice. Use one seeded NumPy Generator, one CPU, and no filesystem or network I/O. Do not depend on the unknown signature of the pre-imported evaluate_erdos_solution helper; implement the exact scoring formula in the program. Do not copy, serialize, reconstruct, or hard-code any entries of initial_h_values, and do not mutate that global.

3.2. Runtime resolution, parent, and fallbacks. Read initial_h_values with a guarded lookup in globals. If it converts to a one-dimensional float64 array of length at least one, that length fixes n even if some parent entries are invalid; ignore a conflicting kwargs n_points. Make a local copy. If the parent is finite and already satisfies the box and mass conditions, use it unchanged as the first start and retain it as a fallback. Otherwise, if it is finite and safely projectable, project it onto K and retain the repaired parent as the parent-derived fallback. Treat a nonfinite parent or a failed projection as unusable, but keep its one-dimensional length as n when available and use the constant fallback at that length. If there is no usable one-dimensional parent length, accept kwargs n_points only as an integer from 8 through 512; otherwise use n=80. Never change a parent’s resolution.

Always create h_const[i]=0.5, which is feasible for every positive n. Keep independent copies of the constant fallback, any repaired parent fallback, and the current global incumbent. Set S and dx only after n is fixed. For n=1 return the best feasible fallback without pair search. Parse seed as an integer; if it is None or conversion fails, use 42.

3.3. Feasibility and projection helpers. Implement a top-level feasibility predicate that requires a one-dimensional finite float64-compatible vector of length n, exact coordinate bounds 0 ≤ h[i] ≤ 1, and abs(sum(h)-S) ≤ 1e-10. Use it for every start, pair proposal, stored incumbent, fallback, and final vector.

Implement project_capped_simplex(z,S). Reject empty, wrong-shaped, nonfinite, or extreme-magnitude inputs; a safe magnitude limit of 1e12 is sufficient for the supplied sizes. Set low=min(z)-1 and high=max(z), so clipping z-low gives all ones and clipping z-high gives all zeros. Perform 80 bisection steps using mid=low+0.5*(high-low); form y=clip(z-mid,0,1); if sum(y)>S move low to mid, otherwise move high to mid. Then correct the residual S-sum(y) using only available slack: for a positive residual add at most 1-y[i] to coordinates below one; for a negative residual subtract at most y[i] from coordinates above zero. Recompute the sum and make further slack-respecting corrections if needed. Return failure unless all values are finite, bounds hold, and mass error is at most 1e-10. This handles odd n, for which S is a half-integer. Never repair by sequential clipping and rescaling.

3.4. Exact scoring and raw lag helper. Implement a top-level helper that first applies the feasibility predicate, then computes corr=np.correlate(h,1-h,mode='full') and values=corr*(2.0/n). Return the finite Python float max(values), and, when useful to the line search, also return raw lag values B in increasing-d order as corr[::-1].copy(). Under NumPy’s linear-correlation indexing the entry for d is at correlation lag -d, which is why reversing gives the specified B_d order. The score is the authoritative evaluator formula; it includes all lags and no circular terms. Return failure for malformed, infeasible, or nonfinite candidates or scores.

3.5. Feasible starts. Score the constant fallback and repaired parent fallback first and use the lowest exact-scored one as the initial incumbent. Build no more than six distinct starts, discarding candidates whose maximum coordinate difference from an existing start is below 1e-10. If a usable parent exists, offer it first, then its reversal, the constant vector, a projected parent perturbation parent+0.12·g with independent standard-normal g, a projected periodic proposal, and a balanced binary proposal. For the periodic proposal choose q uniformly from 1 through min(8,max(1,floor(n/2))) and phase φ uniformly in [0,2π); set z[i]=0.5+0.45 cos(2πqi/n+φ), then project. For the balanced proposal randomly permute coordinates, set floor(n/2) entries to one, and, if n is odd, set one additional entry to 0.5; the rest are zero.

Without a usable parent, offer the constant vector, two independently seeded periodic proposals, a projected 0.5+0.30g proposal, a projected independent uniform-[0,1] proposal, and a balanced proposal. Validate and exactly score every retained start; any start better than the incumbent replaces it with a copy. Construction is algorithmic and uses no literal arrays. If n>128, skip optimization and return the best exact-scored feasible parent or constant fallback at the original resolution.

3.6. Pair schedule. For 2 ≤ n ≤ 128, create a deterministic sparse pair list. Set offsets to every power of two not exceeding floor(n/2), and also include floor(n/2) if it is not already present. For each offset and each i, form the unordered pair {i,(i+offset) mod n}; discard self-pairs and duplicates and sort the resulting pairs. Offset one makes the graph connected; larger offsets add long-range directions. Shuffle a copy of this list with the seeded Generator for each sweep. This list is a work-saving heuristic, not a claim that all feasible descent directions are covered.

Also define the full list of all unordered pairs p<q. The total pair-line-search budget is Btot=min(8000,max(500,floor(64,000,000/(n*n)))). If the full-list size n(n-1)/2 is no greater than Btot, reserve one full-list sweep before running the multistart sparse phase. Otherwise use the whole budget for the sparse phase and do not run the full sweep. This leaves a deterministic, explicit budget for an exhaustive pair-direction pass at the supplied n=80 size while reducing work as n grows.

3.7. Exact line-minimization helper. Implement a top-level helper pair_line_minimum(h,raw,p,q) returning t or failure. Compute t_lo and t_hi from section 2; reject nonfinite or degenerate intervals. For every d in increasing order, compute b_d=g[d,p]-g[d,q] using the coordinate-gradient formula in section 2 and c_d=raw[d+n-1]. Set a_d to -2 at d=0, +1 at d=±(q-p), and zero elsewhere. Verify the arrays are finite.

Build the upper hull of the affine curves for which a_d=0. Sort their slopes b_d using NumPy argsort; for equal slopes retain only the largest intercept c_d. Process lines in increasing slope. For each new line, its crossing with the last hull line is x=(c_last-c_new)/(b_new-b_last). Pop the last line while x is no greater than its stored start; append the new line with that crossing as its start. The first hull start is -∞. Handle a nonfinite crossing as a signed infinity according to the numerator, or reject the line search if its hull cannot be represented safely. If there are no affine lines, use an empty hull and treat L(t) as -∞. This standard upper-line hull gives the maximum of all affine lag curves with at most one active line per segment.

Use a top-level quadratic_roots(A,B,C) helper for intersections. Treat a sufficiently small A relative to max(1,abs(B),abs(C)) as linear; if both A and B are negligible there is no isolated root. Otherwise compute the discriminant, reject it if below a scale-aware negative tolerance, and clamp a small negative discriminant to zero. Use the stable quadratic formula qv=-0.5*(B+copysign(sqrt(discriminant),B)); return qv/A and C/qv, with the repeated-root case handled separately. Discard nonfinite roots.

Construct a candidate list containing t_lo, t_hi, and zero. Add every hull breakpoint in the interval. For each active hull segment clipped to [t_lo,t_hi], add the real roots within that segment of each special Q_d minus that segment’s active line. Add all real pairwise intersections of the three special quadratics that lie in the feasible interval. Add the vertex -b_d/(2a_d) of each special quadratic with a_d>0 when it lies in the interval. Clamp roots that are only within a small scale-aware boundary tolerance to the relevant interval endpoint; discard roots farther outside. Sort finite candidates; duplicate candidates may be retained or removed only when exactly equal.

At each candidate t, evaluate the line envelope by binary search in the hull start array and evaluate the three special quadratics. Their maximum is F(t). Select the candidate with the smallest F; on an exact tie choose the one with smaller abs(t), so zero is preferred on a flat tie. If there is no hull, take the maximum of the three quadratics. The candidate construction is sufficient because the active branch is fixed between consecutive crossings and hull breakpoints: a line or concave quadratic minimizes at an endpoint, and a convex quadratic can additionally minimize only at its vertex. This solves the restricted one-dimensional problem globally up to floating-point arithmetic; it does not solve the full n-dimensional problem globally.

3.8. Multistart coordinate search and acceptance. Initialize the exact-scored incumbent from the fallbacks and starts. For each retained start, set current h to a copy of that start and obtain its exact score and raw lag vector from the scoring helper. Run at most three sparse sweeps. For each shuffled pair, increment the global pair-trial counter and stop the sparse phase if its reserved budget is exhausted. Compute t with pair_line_minimum; skip failures and t values indistinguishable from zero at 1e-14 scale.

Construct a trial by transferring t from q to p. To avoid endpoint roundoff, let pair_sum=h[p]+h[q], set p_new=clip(h[p]+t,max(0,pair_sum-1),min(1,pair_sum)), and set q_new=pair_sum-p_new. Place those values in a copy of h. If it fails feasibility, project the whole trial with project_capped_simplex; reject it if projection fails or feasibility still fails. Score every resulting proposal with the exact correlation helper, never with the line model alone. Save any proposal whose exact score is strictly lower than the global incumbent score. Replace the current coordinate-search state only if its exact score is lower than the current score by more than 1e-13·max(1,abs(current_score)); this makes the local trajectory monotone and prevents roundoff-level cycling. On acceptance, store the raw lag vector freshly returned by the scorer. On rejection, keep the current state and raw lags unchanged.

After a sparse sweep with no accepted move, increment a stagnant-sweep counter; reset it after any acceptance. Stop that start after two consecutive stagnant sweeps or after three sweeps. A failed pair operation rejects only that pair. A start failure must not erase the incumbent or fallback. Every start is scored and compared even if the shared trial budget prevents it from receiving a full sweep.

If the full-pair budget was reserved, start from a copy of the best exact-scored incumbent after the sparse phase. Shuffle all unordered pairs and perform one full sweep using the same exact line minimization, feasibility checks, and monotone exact-score acceptance. Permit one additional full sweep only if the first accepted at least one move and the remaining global budget can cover the entire sweep. Stop after a full sweep with no accepted move or when the budget is exhausted. Keep the incumbent separate from the current full-sweep state; no proposal can worsen the returned incumbent. All budgets and stopping rules execute inside run.

3.9. Final selection. Form a pool from the global incumbent, the repaired parent fallback if available, and the constant fallback. For each candidate, validate it; if it needs numerical mass restoration, project it jointly and validate again. Recompute its exact evaluator score after any repair. Select the feasible pool member with the smallest freshly computed exact score. If search or candidate processing fails, retain the best feasible exact-scored candidate already stored. If all processing fails, return the constant vector at the established resolution with its freshly computed exact score.

4. Search choices and useful variations

Correctness requirements are fixed: retain the supplied parent’s resolution; use the 2n-1 finite-support lags in the exact np.correlate score; jointly enforce 0≤h≤1 and sum(h)=n/2; include both pair-transfer directions through the signed interval; and make all acceptance and final-selection decisions using exact scores. Keep the parent-derived feasible fallback whenever possible. The projection formula and the finite candidate-set line search are not tunable substitutes for another approximate objective.

The default is seed 42, n=80 if there is no usable parent, at most six starts, 80 projection bisections, mass tolerance 1e-10, the dyadic-plus-half sparse pair graph, three sparse sweeps per start, two stagnant sweeps for early stopping, and Btot=min(8000,max(500,floor(64,000,000/n²))). Reserve a full all-pairs pass whenever it fits the budget, with at most one additional pass after improvement. Skip search above n=128 but preserve and score the parent at its original resolution. These choices require no preliminary experiments.

Reasonable fixed variations are 4-6 starts, 2-4 sparse sweeps, a perturbation scale from 0.08 to 0.25, and a total correlation-work cap between roughly 32 million and 80 million multiply-adds. A coder may add a small number of algorithmically generated long-range pairs, provided the cap and full-pair reserve remain explicit. Such choices are heuristics, not evidence of better performance. Any score-dependent stopping or extra pass must follow an explicit in-program rule such as the stagnation and budget rules above; do not tune from external measurements or claim the target has been attained.

5. Numerical robustness and memory use

Use float64 throughout. For the supplied n=80, there are 159 raw lag values; at the optimization ceiling n=128 there are 255. The line hull, roots, candidate points, current vector, trials, and fallbacks all require O(n) storage. The pair list is O(n log n), and np.correlate produces only O(n) output. Do not construct an n-by-n product table, Hessian, dense solver model, or lag-gradient matrix. Each exact correlation is O(n²); Btot limits the number of pair line searches to approximately O(64,000,000/n²), capped at 8000, and optimization is skipped above n=128. Run serially on one CPU; do not assume a GPU or extra processors.

Reject nonfinite parents, starts, lag coefficients, hull data, roots, trials, and scores. Use the stable quadratic formula and scale-aware discriminant tolerance. The feasible t interval is bounded by coordinate slack, so candidate roots outside it are discarded. Treat a failed hull or root calculation as a rejected line search, not a reason to corrupt the current state. Projection and pair construction must preserve box bounds; residual correction uses only slack. Recompute the exact raw lags after every accepted move to prevent model-rounding drift. If a proposal is infeasible, projection fails, or its exact score is nonfinite, reject it and keep the best stored feasible candidate.

6. Runtime safeguards and return contract

The generated program must expose run(seed=42, **kwargs) at top level and return exactly (h_values, c5_bound, n_points). At runtime, check parent dimensionality, length, and finite values before use. Check every start, pair proposal, stored incumbent, fallback, and final candidate for finite values, exact bounds 0≤h[i]≤1, and absolute mass error at most 1e-10. A failed candidate check means rejection or joint projection followed by a second check; never accept an invalid candidate.

Before returning, choose only from validated candidates and recompute c5_bound inside the program as float(max(np.correlate(h_values,1-h_values,mode='full')*(2.0/n_points))). Do not return a line-search model value, cached stale score, surrogate, or assumed target. Return h_values as a finite float64 NumPy vector, c5_bound as a finite Python float, and n_points as an integer equal to len(h_values). If any search operation fails, return the best exact-scored feasible candidate accumulated so far; if none survives, return the constant feasible fallback and its freshly computed exact score. The generated program performs no filesystem or network I/O and makes no claim that it has attained a particular bound.
